title: Prototype Pattern
summary: Cloning an existing, already-configured object instead of building one from scratch — and why shallow vs deep copy is where nearly every bug in this pattern lives.

slides.markdown: **Prototype** creates new objects by copying an existing, fully-configured instance rather than building one from scratch through a constructor or factory. It's the pattern to reach for when construction is expensive, or when the "right" configuration only exists at runtime as an already-built object — clone it, then tweak the copy. The entire pattern lives or dies on getting the *copy* right: shallow vs deep cloning is where most Prototype bugs come from.

slides.sectionTitle: Prototype: cloning an existing object instead of building from scratch
slides.markdown:
**Prototype** defines a `clone()` method that returns a new object with the same field values as the original, instead of a caller running the original construction path again.

```java
RobotConfig heavyUnit = loadFromDisk("heavy-unit.cfg"); // expensive: disk + parsing
RobotConfig anotherHeavy = heavyUnit.clone();             // cheap: memory copy
anotherHeavy.setName("Unit-02");
```

The caller never re-runs the expensive disk read and parsing that built `heavyUnit` — cloning copies the already-computed result, then only the differing fields get changed.

Takeaway: Prototype replaces "build it again" with "copy it, then adjust," which only pays off when building it again is genuinely expensive or awkward.

slides.sectionTitle: Shallow copy vs deep copy — where clone bugs actually come from
slides.markdown:
A **shallow copy** duplicates an object's own fields, but if a field holds a reference to another object — a list, a nested object — the copy gets the *same reference*, so both the original and the clone point at the same underlying object.

A **deep copy** recursively clones referenced objects too, so the clone owns entirely independent data all the way down.

This is where nearly every Prototype bug lives: `clonedConfig.getTags().add("x")` on a shallow copy silently mutates the *original's* tag list too, since both share the same `List` instance. The bug shows up far from the clone call, as a mysterious change to an object nobody touched directly.

Takeaway: before shipping a `clone()` method, know exactly which fields are shared references and decide, deliberately, whether that's safe.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: shallow vs deep clone of an object graph
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: an original object with a nested mutable list; a shallow-clone arrow pointing at the same shared list box as the original; a deep-clone arrow pointing at its own separate copy of the list box >>>

The diagram makes the bug visible: a shallow clone's arrow to its nested list lands on the *same box* as the original's arrow — one mutation, two objects affected. A deep clone's arrow lands on a freshly copied box that only it owns.

This is the single fact to check before trusting any `clone()` implementation: follow each reference field's arrow and confirm where it actually points.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: implementing a correct deep-copy clone
When Prototype beats a factory: expensive construction, runtime-configured templates
slides.markdown:
Prototype wins over a factory in two situations. First, **expensive construction**: if building an object means a disk read, a network call, or heavy computation, cloning an already-built instance is far cheaper than re-running that construction path.

Second, **runtime-configured templates**: sometimes the "recipe" for an object only exists as data assembled at runtime — a user-customized loadout, an A/B-tested product configuration — not as a fixed set of constructor arguments a factory could take. A factory needs to know its parameters in advance; Prototype just needs an already-correct instance to copy.

Takeaway: reach for Prototype when the *thing you'd copy* already exists and building it fresh would be genuinely wasteful or awkward to parameterize.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a "deep" clone that misses a nested mutable field
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I wrote a deep-copy `clone()` method, so mutating the clone can never affect the original."

**Why it's wrong:** "deep copy" only holds for fields the developer actually remembered to copy. Add a new mutable field to the class later — say, a `Map<String, String> metadata` — and forget to update `clone()`, and that one field silently reverts to shallow-copy behavior: the clone and original share the same map, and a bug reappears exactly where the last one was fixed.

**Correct model:** treat every new mutable reference field as a required update to `clone()`, and verify it with a test that mutates the clone and asserts the original is unaffected — for every reference field, not just the ones that existed when `clone()` was first written.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: Prototype vs Builder vs Factory Method for object creation
slides.markdown:
All three create objects, but they answer different questions about *what* gets created and from what starting point.

| | Starting point | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Factory Method | Nothing — builds fresh via a subclass decision | Choosing *which* class, cheaply built from scratch |
| Builder | Nothing — assembles fresh, step by step | One complex object with many optional parts |
| Prototype | An existing, already-built instance | Copying something expensive or runtime-configured, then tweaking it |

**How to decide:** if construction is cheap and the parameters are known upfront, use Factory Method or Builder. If the "correct" starting point only exists as an already-built object — because building it is expensive or its configuration was assembled at runtime — Prototype is the only one of the three that avoids rebuilding it.
